title: US Leading Economic Index Slips in June as Consumer Spending Weakens, Reversing Two Months of Gains
excerpt: The Conference Board’s predictive gauge fell 0.2% to 99.1, dragged down by declining consumer expectations and a drop in building permits, though AI investment is expected to cushion the economy.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The Leading Economic Index fell 0.2% to 99.1 in June, reversing previous gains.
  • Weak consumer expectations and declining building permits significantly impacted the index.
  • The LEI is down only 0.3% for the first half of 2026, improving from last year's contraction.
  • Strong AI investment is expected to support economic activity despite softening consumer spending.

  • The Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index (LEI) fell 0.2% to 99.1 in June, partially reversing gains from April and May
  • Weak consumer expectations and a drop in building permits were the largest drags on the index
  • The LEI is down only 0.3% for the first half of 2026, a significant improvement over the 1.1% contraction in the second half of 2025
  • Strong business investment in artificial intelligence is expected to support economic activity even as consumer spending softens

U.S. leading economic indicators edged lower in June, signaling that consumer spending is losing steam even as business investment in artificial intelligence helps keep the broader economy afloat.

The Leading Economic Index, published by the Conference Board, slid 0.2% to 99.1, following a 0.1% increase in May and a 0.2% increase in April. While the prior two months’ gains were partially reversed, the index is down just 0.3% for the first half of 2026 — a marked improvement over the 1.1% contraction recorded in the second half of 2025.

What Dragged the Index Down

The largest negative contributions came from weakening consumer expectations and a decline in building permits, according to Justyna Zabinska-La Monica, a senior manager at the Conference Board. Financial components provided the biggest positive lift, led by the yield spread, but it wasn’t enough to offset the consumer-side weakness.

The LEI’s six-month and 12-month growth rates both remain negative, though they have stabilized — a pattern consistent with an economy that is slowing but not collapsing.

The index is based on 10 components, including manufacturers’ new orders, building permits for new private housing, stock prices, and consumer expectations. It is designed to signal shifts in the business cycle before they show up in harder economic data.

AI Investment as Economic Cushion

One bright spot: business investment in artificial intelligence continues to run hot, and the Conference Board expects it to support economic activity even as consumers pull back. Companies across sectors have ramped up capital expenditure on AI infrastructure, a trend reflected in recent earnings from major tech firms.

“Consumer spending is weakening, though strong business investment in artificial intelligence is expected to hold economic activity afloat while inflation improves.”

— The Conference Board

The Conference Board has also raised its GDP guidance despite the LEI slip, suggesting that the broader economic picture remains more resilient than the headline index number might imply.

Global Context

The U.S. reading comes alongside mixed signals from other major economies. India’s LEI rose 0.9% in the most recent reading, one of the stronger performances globally. China’s index ticked down 0.1%, with consumer expectations remaining below the neutral threshold for over four years. The Euro Area LEI fell 0.3% in June, extending its downtrend.

Mexico’s LEI plunged 2.1% — the steepest decline among major economies tracked by the Conference Board — driven by falling crude oil prices and weak manufacturing inventories.

What It Means for NRI Investors

For Indian professionals and investors in the United States, the softening consumer outlook bears watching. Housing-related indicators, including building permits, directly affect real estate markets in metro areas with large Indian-American populations. The tech sector’s AI-driven spending boom offers some insulation for those working in technology, but broader economic weakness could slow hiring and compress wage growth in other sectors.

Markets largely shrugged off the data, with investors focused on upcoming earnings reports and the Federal Reserve’s next policy meeting. The Conference Board’s next LEI release is scheduled for August.
